📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Update for 2:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 23: On Sunday afternoon (Nov. 22), the BepiColombo team announced that, while the spacecraft did successfully arrive in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), the engine burn that got it there was cut short due to a software glitch. On Monday (Nov. 23), we got another update: BepiColombo "is safe and in a stable orbit around Mercury" and is on track for the next big milestone: The separation of its two orbiters on Dec. 9.

For just the second time ever, Mercury has received a robotic visitor from Earth.

It has been revealed that the BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — arrived in orbit around Mercury on Saturday (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.

Before BepiColombo, just one spacecraft had ever circled the solar system's innermost planet: NASA's MESSENGER, which did so from March 2011 to April 2015.

BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

The duo released — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018, beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system.

Mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun. Spacecraft approaching the planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must therefore shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug.

According to recent reports, so the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year, however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters.

Saturday's orbital insertion came after a 37-minute-long engine burn, which began at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT). There was a bit drama involved, however, as confirmation of the maneuver's success didn't come for several hours afterward.

"We've heard back from Bepi — the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC [the European Space Operations Centre] are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next update with the upcoming steps," the mission team noted via X on Saturday evening.

We've heard back from Bepi - the spacecraft is now in contact with the ground and the teams at ESOC are busy assessing the telemetry. Flight Dynamics already has confirmed it achieved orbital capture around Mercury! Early next week we'll share the next revision with the upcoming steps.November 22, 2026.

Orbital insertion is the latest milestone in BepiColombo's Mercury arrival phase, which is expected to take about six months in total.

Arrival began on Sept. 3, when the MTM released MPO and Mio. The two orbiters remain connected today; they won't separate until Dec. 9 or thereabouts.

Industry observers note that shortly thereafter, Mio will settle into its final orbit, a highly elliptical path that will take it over Mercury's poles. MPO is also destined for a polar orbit, though a much less elliptical one than Mio's; the ESA probe will conduct a series of engine burns before finally getting there on March 10, 2027.

Sources indicate that bepiColombo — which is named after the late Italian scientist and mathematician Giuseppe "Bepi" Colombo — won't start doing science work until April 6, 2027. The two probes will gather complementary data from their different vantage points, shedding a great deal of light on a mysterious world.

"The mission will study all aspects of Mercury, from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind, to its internal structure with its large iron core, and the origin of the planet’s magnetic field," ESA officials wrote in a BepiColombo mission description.

"The data will enable scientists to understand more about the origin and evolution of a planet located close to its parent star, and a better understanding of the overall evolution of our solar system," they added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Brady knows that all parents drop the ball sometimes.

Since becoming dad to son Jack, 19, with ex-girlfriend Bridget Moynahan, as well as son Benjamin, 16, and daughter Vivian, 13, with ex-wife Gisele Bündchen, the seven-time Super Bowl champ admitted there are some losses among his many wins as a parent.

“Well, I’ve made a lot of mistakes,” Brady said on the Nov. 22 episode of the High Performance podcast. “So, a lot like quarterback. I threw a lot of interceptions. And with every one I’ve tried to learn.”.

In a recent development, and with that effort, the 49-year-old added, “I hope I’m a better parent today than I was when I first started having kids. And hopefully I’m a better parent 10 years from now.”.

So, what is Brady’s game proposal for becoming the best dad he can be?

It has been revealed that “The crucial thing for me in my personal life is to go where my kids are at, too,” he explained. “Not to say, ‘Hey kids, pay attention to the things I'm doing or what's important to me.’ It’s been a really important lesson for me over the years to go to my kids and say, ‘What’s really important to you? #185228. Breaking: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

Breaking: A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1413 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
  • Industry observers note that the findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.
  • Industry observers note that the discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

Industry observers note that the findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to fresh treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

Industry observers note that the discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's.

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Recent findings suggest that previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," noted Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease.".

According to recent reports, to investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage.

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One important effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

In a recent development, beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," said Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see.".

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse.

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

According to recent reports, the results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," said Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies.".

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an crucial protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments.

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

Recent findings suggest that they combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," mentioned Huijie Huang.

According to recent reports, plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies.".

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research.

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

Sources indicate that the team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," said Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment.".

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal newly introduced treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

SpaceX will retire 1st Starship upper stage ever caught by 'chopsticks,' Elon Musk claims

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.
  • According to recent reports, that vehicle, known as Ship 42, rolled out Nov.
  • Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again.

According to recent reports, that vehicle, known as Ship 42, rolled out Nov. 13 on Starship's 15th test flight. A day later, it returned from orbit, nestling softly into the "chopstick" arms of its launch tower at SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas.

Ship 42 made it through Flight 15 in good condition, according to SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who said it "could probably be reflown with a few weeks of refurbishment." But that's not going to happen.

Recent findings suggest that "In this case, because it's kind of an historic ship, we're going to, I think, not take any chances with the ship and just kind of leave it for public display, because what it's done is historic," Musk mentioned on Wednesday (Nov. 18) during a discussion at the TomorrowX Summit.

Industry observers note that he didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. (SpaceX plans to shift most Starship releases to its new Starbase Louisiana site, but construction has yet to begin on that $100 billion complex.).

According to recent reports, musk participated virtually in the TomorrowX conversation, which was moderated by two friends of his, the venture capitalists Gavin Baker and Antonio Gracias. (TomorrowX took place in Austin, Texas, but Musk was in China on Wednesday as part of President Trump's delegation for his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.).

The world's richest man expounded on Ship 42's historic achievement, explaining that it gets SpaceX much closer to the "holy grail of rocketry" — a fully and rapidly reusable launch vehicle.

Recent findings suggest that before Flight 15, SpaceX had already caught Starship's first-stage booster, known as Super Heavy, on three separate occasions, and it had reflown a booster twice. But the tech giant had never attempted a Ship catch, which is a taller order, given how much faster and farther Starship upper stages fly.

So snagging Ship on the first try was a very big deal, according to Musk.

"Everyone knew, within SpaceX, at least, how key this milestone was, and that it was really something fundamental and profound — that Starship will be the first-ever fully reusable orbital space system," he told Baker and Gracias on Wednesday.

According to recent reports, and SpaceX is very serious about Starship reuse. Musk has said that the organization wants to launch about 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030.

This mind-boggling cadence will help the company build out two enormous megaconstellations in low Earth orbit — the next iteration of its Starlink broadband network, which will consist of about 100,000 satellites, and its Starmind AI data-center constellation, which will be 10 times bigger than that.

Assembly of that latest Starlink network is already underway. Ship carried 26 of the next-gen internet spacecraft up for the first time on Flight 14, which introduced on Sept. 28, and repeated the feat on Flight 15.

Home Depot on Tuesday declared its chief financial officer, Richard McPhail, will become CEO of the organization, succeeding Ted Decker, effective next week.

Alongside McPhail's appointment, Home Depot mentioned Ann-Marie Campbell, currently senior executive vice president of U.S. stores and operations, will become president and chief operating officer. Jordan Broggi has been chosen as CFO to succeed McPhail.

It has been revealed that decker, CEO since 2022, had been on temporary medical leave since August. The organization said on Tuesday that Decker has returned from leave but is now stepping down from his role. He will continue to serve as chair of the board of directors, the company said.

Sources indicate that "I'm glad to be back and grateful for the support I received," Decker told analysts on Tuesday. "The board and I have agreed that now is the right time to move to the next phase of our succession proposal.".

McPhail has been with the tech giant since 2005, holding multiple executive roles.

"We're not going to change course," McPhail told CNBC's Becky Quick.

Recent findings suggest that he said the manufacturer will continue to lean into winning professional shoppers like contractors and using artificial intelligence tools to encourage sales. McPhail added that while the company faces more challenges now than it did at the start of the year, it is still winning share of the home improvement market.

In a recent development, home Depot has been pressured by a sluggish housing market, higher mortgage rates and a more cautious consumer. Still, the manufacturer has previously noted it's seen resilience among its pro shoppers who are still shopping for their home improvement projects.

Shares of Home Depot sank more than 3% following the announcement and the retailer's fiscal third-quarter results.

Recent findings suggest that the CEO change came as the home improvement retailer posted quarterly earnings and revenue that beat analysts' expectations. The company stated comparable sales rose 2.2% during the period, compared with estimates of up 1.8%, according to StreetAccount.

Here's how Home Depot performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

In a recent development, the tech giant reported net income of $3.71 billion, or $3.72 per share, compared with $3.60 billion, or $3.62 per share, the year prior. Excluding one-time items, Home Depot reported adjusted earnings per share of $3.86.

Revenue rose 4.9% compared with the year-ago period.

"We also are confident that we are taking material share from the market and from competition," McPhail said on the call with analysts.

In the third quarter, the manufacturer said online comparable sales grew around 13%, which marked its sixth straight quarter of double-digit positive growth for the metric.

The company mentioned it saw positive comparable sales numbers in 13 out of 16 of its merchandising departments, including notable strength in the power department, which posted double-digit percentage growth.

For the full year, Home Depot stated it expects total sales to rise roughly 4.5%, the top end of its previously provided range. It also anticipates comparable sales will grow around 1.4%, compared with an outlook of flat to a 2% increase.

Home Depot added it expects adjusted earnings per share to rise 2% this year, compared with prior guidance of flat to a 4% increase.

Breaking: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, vitamin C may do more than support everyday health.
  • According to recent reports, exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades.
  • One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

According to recent reports, exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to crucial functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation.

"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies.".

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

In a recent development, their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

Could Taking Vitamin C After Meals Help?

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

It has been revealed that their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

Upcoming Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research.

According to recent reports, the researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

Recent findings suggest that "This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur.".

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet another former member of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) appears to have exited the government only to return as a contractor.

In September, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) put out a call for a contract worth $200,000 for “modernization discovery, prototyping, and implementation-planning engagement.” Four days later, the department closed the bidding process and awarded the contract to Yat Choi LLC, a manufacturer owned by a former Airbnb engineer and Canadian citizen named Yat Choi, whose company also goes by the name GovMaxxing.

Recent findings suggest that at the time, Choi had left his role at the National Design Studio (NDS)—the group tasked with redesigning government websites—just a few weeks prior. Before that, Choi worked at DOGE.

Recent findings suggest that the bid was for a project set to run for a little under six months, and the contract was awarded as sole-source, meaning that it did not go through a normal competitive bidding process. In the documentation announcing the award, HHS justified this decision by saying that its “market research and source rationale found that conventional consulting firms generally would need to assemble a multidisciplinary team or obtain additional technical resources” to provide the required skills around “business-process modernization, artificial intelligence, automation, technical architecture, and rapid prototyping.”.

According to recent reports, in October, a company called CoA Solutions lodged what’s known as a bid protest with the Government Accountability Office (GAO) contesting the agency’s decision to award the contract to Choi. CoA Solutions is a small business that builds AI software for the government and received another contract with the Treasury Department in 2024.

Ari Perez, the CEO of CoA Solutions, tells WIRED that his company made a bid below the $200,000 award price, and it proposed two experts doing the work full-time, including Perez himself.

Industry observers note that perez states that CoA asked HHS for an explanation of the award on October 8 and, when it did not receive one, filed its protest with the GAO the next day. Perez says that his manufacturer’s sole contestation was about how the bids were evaluated by HHS, not about Choi or his work with NDS.

Sources indicate that “I'm a service-disabled veteran. I've served this government since I was 17 at West Point. At the US Digital Service I helped deliver for veterans at the VA, and later I worked on asylum and immigration systems at DHS. I started CoA to keep doing impactful government work,” states Perez. “We want to win on merit, and if HHS reopens it, we'll bid again.”.

According to CoA, in response to the bid protest, HHS terminated the award to Choi and canceled the call for contractors. With the cancellation, the GAO dismissed the protest without investigating it further. A GAO spokesperson referred WIRED to HHS.

In a recent development, “HHS remains committed to modernizing its systems to improve efficiency and better serve the American people,” claims HHS spokesperson Grace Davis Jamison. “Following a bid protest challenging the award, HHS voluntarily took corrective action, terminating the contract at no cost to the government and canceling the solicitation.”.

Sources indicate that choi’s role in the US government has not been exactly clear. In his bio on X, Choi writes that he was part of both DOGE and NDS, and stated in a post that he was recruited by billionaire Elon Musk and Joe Gebbia, Airbnb’s cofounder, to help modernize the retirement system at the Office of Personnel Management (OPM). Gebbia now leads NDS, which was created after Musk left government and which has served as a landing pad for several DOGE members, including Edward “Big Balls” Coristine.

Recent findings suggest that in December 2025, Choi contributed to a blog on the NDS website about automating the federal retirement system. But on his LinkedIn, Choi lists himself as a senior technologist at OPM. On November 5, just two days after Republicans lost the midterm elections, Choi revealed in a post on X that he had left OPM and was launching his manufacturer, GovMaxxing, through which he plans to continue to contract with the government. GovMaxxing operates as Yat Choi LLC federally.

It has been revealed that in response to questions from WIRED about his role in government, Choi indicates that he “was recruited to support federal modernization efforts and subsequently onboarded as an OPM contractor.” There, Choi says, he “contributed to modernization efforts associated with DOGE and subsequently NDS. I was not, and have never been, a federal government employee.” Choi claims he left OPM in mid-August, though OPM did not respond to questions confirming whether this was the case. “I began actively pursuing the contracting opportunity after my engagement with OPM ended,” says Choi.

In a recent development, choi confirmed that he is a Canadian citizen and a “lawful permanent resident” of the US. Foreigners are not generally allowed to hold full-time roles in government or serve as special government employees. The rules are more flexible for contractors. During the height of DOGE’s activity, a close Musk ally, Baris Akis, was prevented from joining the group as a special government employee because he is a Turkish citizen, according to The Atlantic. Akis, however, continued to serve as a recruiter for the group.

On his website, Choi labels the “client” for his work in government as “US Office of Personnel Management / DOGE / National Design Studio” and describes himself as the “modernization lead.” However, documents indicate that Choi’s firm was not registered in the state of Fresh York until April 2026, and in the System for Award Management, the procurement website where US government contractors bid, there are no other contracts for Choi’s work. “None of my work at OPM was performed through my LLC. My website references my prior professional experience at OPM and does not attribute that work to my company,” claims Choi.

Choi says that the HHS contract was for a “separate modernization discovery project. It was not a continuation of any work with OPM, DOGE, or NDS.”.

According to the code of federal regulations, except in very specific circumstances, government contracts cannot be awarded to government employees or to organizations they fully or partially own. But Jessica Tillipman, associate dean for government procurement law studies at George Washington University, says that even though Choi was not a regular government employee, the fact that he was part of DOGE and NDS, whose work has spanned across government agencies, could create the appearance of a conflict of interest with regard to the HHS contract. “The baseline posture of the federal acquisition regulation is to strictly avoid conflicts of interest or even the appearance of them,” says Tillipman. “So agencies all have a duty, and the contracting teams have a duty, to make sure that they are considering these things when they're awarding these contracts.”.

Recent findings suggest that choi tells WIRED that HHS “initiated contact and expressed interest” in his “modernization experience” before the call for bids was declared. HHS did not respond to questions about whether the bid had been written specifically for him.

Recent findings suggest that tillipman notes that while the government may sometimes create a contracting opportunity designed for a specific person or manufacturer, “it’s generally niche or highly specialized work." Tillipman states that the fact that there were 75 bids placed on the contract indicates that this is “not a unique service.” She notes that the government’s justification for a sole-source contract is “thin.” “Usually, when there's only one responsible source, there's a technical reason,” she says. This could be something like a special tool that is not interoperable with outside software, or when there is only one company that can provide a specific service or that makes a certain physical part that might be used for weapons or specialized machinery.

On the GovMaxxing website, Choi notes that potential government clients can work with the tech giant as a prime contractor or “subcontract through one of our partner primes your agency may already be working with.” Unlike prime contracts, there is no way to publicly see which subcontractor a prime contractor works with. Choi declined to name the companies or current “prime” contractors he subcontracts under.

According to recent reports, but Tillipman indicates that even if Choi were to take on another version of the HHS contract for a subcontractor, similar questions could still be raised within the agency and externally should it ever come to light. “In certain instances, your subcontractors’ conflicts can be imputed to the prime contractor,” she says. “The whole thing is highly irregular overall.”.

Choi is not the only former DOGE or NDS member who appears to be hoping to benefit from federal contracts after leaving the government. Earlier this year, WIRED reported that Ethan Shaotran, one of the young engineers who formed the early core of DOGE, had started a defense tech startup. The startup has been listed on the System for Award Management since April. Former DOGE members Jack Stein, Gavin Kliger, Luke Farritor, and Marko Elez released an AI defense technology firm called Cathedral, which has been listed on the System for Award Management since July. Neither have received “prime” contracts with any federal agency, but whether they have been taken on as subcontractors to other prime contractors is unclear.

Despite the HHS contract’s cancellation, Choi appears undeterred. Earlier this week, following the nationwide grounding of flights by the Federal Aviation Administration, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called for funding to modernize air traffic control in a post on X. In response, Choi wrote, “Secretary Duffy, I’m the DOGE engineer who led the modernization of federal retirement processing at OPM last year … I’ve since started a firm to work with more agencies, and we’d love to help with the FAA’s modernization efforts. Put us in, coach!”.

Tech Report: The 8 best headphones of 2026: We tested the top contenders from Sony, Apple, Bose, and Beats

  • In 2026, a pair of headphones or earbuds is pretty much non-optional.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2026, a pair of headphones or earbuds is pretty much non-optional. That's why there are hundreds of different headphones shapes, sizes, styles, colors, and, of course, prices. These days, you can grab a random pair off the digital shelf without too much research and find that they do the job just fine. However, if you're tired of settling for "just fine," then it's worth investing in the best headphones available.

But be warned: The latest generation of flagship noise-cancelling headphones from the likes of Apple, Sony, and Bose will set you back $450 or more, though we have options to recommend for every price range.

These are the tech, tools, and products — from laptops to e-readers, from earbuds to robovacs, and more — that Mashable ranks best in class.

Recent findings suggest that to help you find the best pair of headphones possible, our experts test headphones year-round, from popular models to new releases to budget picks (you can learn more about our detailed testing standards below). The result of that vetting is this guide, which we keep updated regularly to give you the most accurate and current purchasing information possible. The best tech deal this week The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

Read our full review of the Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones.

Audiophiles and custom equalizer fans: After three years, Sony's flagship wireless headphones finally got an enhancement. If you love Sony headphones and have an old pair of XM4s, then we can definitely recommend an upgrade. However, if you just purchased a pair of XM5s, then it might be harder to justify an instant upgrade. That said, the active noise cancellation is better than ever, and there are noticeable improvements to audio quality (even if they lose out by a smidge to the latest Technics AZ100 earbuds). Besides music lovers, travelers will also appreciate the upcoming Sony cans, as they fold up and come with an improved travel case.

Mashable's Tech Editor Timothy Beck Werth reviewed the XM6 headphones ahead of their launch, and he was impressed with the overall quality. As Werth wrote in his review, "The new Sony headphones offer impressive audio quality, and they definitely improve on the XM5 models. The active noise cancellation is particularly phenomenal...I really appreciated the overall balance, depth, and quality of the audio. For the XM6, Sony audio engineers worked with music mastering engineers here in the United States, and the results are clear when you listen to music. Like all headphone reviewers, I have a dedicated playlist for testing new audio products, and I found that vocal-heavy tracks sound particularly great, with noticeable improvements over the XM5s.".

Sony introduced (or, rather, brought back) a major design change for the XM6 headphones — they fold up for easier storage. They're definitely more compact and easier to travel with compared to the previous-gen model. The overall design looks similar, so if you're a fan of the Sony aesthetic, you'll still appreciate how they look.

It has been revealed that we do wish there had been slightly bigger improvements after a three-year wait, and the battery life (30 hours with ANC engaged) is the same as the XM5 model, which we also loved. These headphones did arrive with a higher sticker price, so if you can't quite swing the $448 price tag, look for the excellent XM5 headphones on sale.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones (2nd gen).

Those who want the best of the best: For anyone who's yet to buy into the Bose QuietComfort Ultra line, but wants noise-cancelling headphones that can easily handle long hours of wear, there's no better choice than the second generation Bose QuietComfort Ultra headphones.

The best noise-cancelling headphones aren't much use if they squeeze your head too tight or prevent you from wearing accessories like earrings or glasses comfortably. In other words, comfort is key — we were substantial fans of Bose's first gen QC Ultra headphones for exactly this reason.

In a recent development, with the second generation of the headphones, Bose makes minor improvements to the soundscape, noise-cancelling, and somehow the wear. They also fixed other bugs that detracted from the otherwise premium experience of using the QC Ultras.

Industry observers note that as a first step, Bose upped the battery life from 24 to 30 hours per charge with ANC. They also added options for wired playback with the USB-C cable (which can simultaneously charge the headphones) or the auxiliary cable for passive playback (which wasn't available on the first gen headphones). In tandem with the battery life, these headphones become much stronger contenders for travel.

According to recent reports, for day-to-day use, Bose's noise cancelling remains as solid as ever (though Sony's XM6s are ever so slightly more adept at handling high pitched frequencies), while offering an easy adjustment on 10 different levels of ANC via the companion app. As for the listening experience, the immersive audio remains as lackluster as it did on the first gen, but the overall sound profile came through richer and more robust when we compared the headphones side by side. Bose also added quality of life adjustments like better wear detection, and a lay flat mode that puts the headphones into a low power mode when they're placed face down. Overall, it's hard to beat this blend of sound quality, ANC, and comfort, making the second iteration of the QC Ultras one of our top picks for headphones.

Industry observers note that value fiends: If you don't particularly care to have the most premium pair of headphones on the market (or care to spend several hundred dollars on them), the JLab JBuds Lux ANC headphones are the best budget headphones available. They have functional ANC, decent comfort, great sound balance, and a killer battery life, all with a design that doesn't feel cheap.

At their regular sale price of around $50, these are about a ninth the price of the latest Sony headphones, and a seventh of the price of the Bose QuietComfort headphones, which feel like these headphones' premium analogue.

With budget headphones, it's good to understand what you're trading off from the jump. In the case of these JLab headphones, the ANC will dampen a good amount of environmental sound, from talking coworkers to loud fans, but it won't completely silence the world around you. The app can lag some (we had to exit out of it a few times during testing when it froze), and the fit of these headphones might not be for everyone. For one of our testers, these headphones squeezed their head more than usual (though some people on Reddit called these the most comfortable headphones they've tried). Regardless of the fit, you're likely to hear some creaking from time to time when you move your head around.

At $80, these are all cons that may not be ideal, but are fair for the price point. At these headphones' frequent sale prices that hover in the $50 to $55 range, these cons are even easier to swallow, especially when you consider how these headphones actually sound.

It has been revealed that to be clear, you'll likely need to play around with the EQ some to find your perfect settings — we found the first preset to be on the bass-heavy end. Once you do, it's impressive the way these headphones can balance a song. Every part of Panic! At The Disco's "Northern Downpour" shone through, from the vocals, lead guitar, bass, and piano. For budget headphones, we might expect some muddying through these elements, but the JLab JBuds held up great. If we're being nitpicky, The Beatles' "In My Life" came through somewhat dimmer sounding than expected, but not necessarily muddy.

In a recent development, beyond the sound signature, these headphones have a reasonable amount of customization with the app, especially for their price point. You can adjust the button commands on one of the three on-ear buttons, adjust the ANC intensity with a slider in the app, and create your own custom EQ settings. Multipoint pairing is available, as are spatial audio, music, and movie modes.

Recent findings suggest that students, casual owners, and anyone looking for great sound on the cheap: The newly introduced price of entry for flagship noise-cancelling headphones? A cool $450, at least. So, if you're looking for wireless headphones with true active noise cancellation but don't want to spend more than $100, then go with Sony's mid-range noise-cancellers on sale. They have Sony's signature sound (and signature all-plastic design, sadly), while still being plenty compact for taking on the go.

Recent findings suggest that sony's sound profile is one of the best found on consumer headphones, and it doesn't require a $450+ price to access. While these mid-range headphones won't offer the same experience as the flagship model, they still offer an impressive degree of clarity and depth, especially when adjusted with the 10-band equalizer in the companion app.

Noise cancellation-wise, don't expect absolute silence. Voices are likely to come through, but normal hums and fans will be blocked out. This is very much a get what you pay for situation. Another give-and-take comes in the design. The placement of the tactile controls is great, as are the folding ear cups for easy transport. Less ideal is the tight squeeze of these headphones, but if you don't anticipate needing extended hours of wear, this likely is no need to detract. Long-haul listeners can take solace in not needing to recharge the battery often — you get 50 hours of playback with ANC powered on, and 75 hours without it.

In a recent development, at $179.99, they're a fair price, but we recommend waiting until you can grab them on sale. At the right time, you can catch them as low as $98.

Read our full review of the Nothing Headphone (a).

In a recent development, folks too busy to charge their devices: If you're just a little too familiar with the low battery sound on your headphones, the absurdly long battery life on the Nothing Headphone (a) gets you as close as you can to a guarantee that you'll hear it as little as possible. Plus, it has a standout retro design.

Picking the headphones with the best battery life isn't a terribly complex process. That stated, it isn't just about picking the pair that can pack the most hours — it's about finding the headphones with the best combination of value, overall performance, and, of course, battery life.

Our standard before was set at 60 hours, which is a great deal higher than the 30 hours you'll find on the Bose and Sony headphones on this list. The Nothing Headphone (a) absolutely blows that standard out of the water, offering 75 hours per charge with ANC on, and 135 hours without.

Recent findings suggest that they check the remaining boxes at $199, which, while not dirt cheap, is a fair deal cheaper than most $400+ flagship models. The sound quality is clear and robust, the noise cancellation will get the job done (if not flawlessly), and the on-ear controls are truly a thing of perfection. During testing, we almost never reached for our devices when adjusting settings because the on-ear controls made it so easy not to. Rounding out the experience is a companion app that's easy to navigate, with features like an eight-band equalizer designed to make your music sound just to your liking.

Read our full review of the Bose QuietComfort headphones (2nd gen).

Travelers, students, and anyone blending comfort and value: A lot about our most comfortable headphones pick sounds great, but you're caught up on the price point — understandable. Though a truly excellent, well-rounded headphones experience often comes with a higher price point, Bose's latest headphones — the second generation QuietComforts — prove that investment doesn't need to exceed $400 (for now).

If you're looking for extreme comfort, quality ANC, warm and balanced sound, and a few extras without totally breaking the bank, these are your headphones.

According to recent reports, these aren't perfect headphones. The sound profile isn't the most customizable with a three-band equalizer, there's no truly passive playback with the wired connections, the noise cancellation will get staticky during a plane takeoff, and the battery life leans on the low side at 24 hours (finding 30 hours or up isn't too hard these days on a pair of over-ear headphones).

All this to say, these aren't technically perfect headphones, but those cons pale in comparison to their pros. At $359, these headphones are nearly $100 cheaper than the Bose QC Ultra 2 headphones, but offer many of the same features. For starters, the comfort and noise cancellation are nearly on par with the significantly more expensive headphones, which is to say it's very, very good — like easily wearable for a full day of travel. The tactile controls are intuitive and functional, the colorways are varied and unique while remaining appealing, and there's an Immersive Audio listening mode for changing up how you hear your music.

In a time when most tech prices are rising, it's refreshing to see a brand release a pair of headphones that strive for ultra-premium performance, while sticking to a more mildly premium price point.

Read our original review of the Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones, or see how they compare to the latest XM6 headphones.

Industry observers note that last-gen lovers: If you want a premium pair of Sony noise-cancelling headphones but refuse to pay more than $400 for a pair of headphones, we feel you. We also have good news: The XM5 headphones hold up well in 2026, and they're still worth the investment, especially when they're on sale.

It has been revealed that originally released in 2022, the Sony XM5 headphones are still legendary. They had unbeatable ANC and sound for the money, and even in 2026, they sound shockingly good. That's because the upcoming flagship XM6 model only made iterative improvements over these cans. So, now that they go on sale for as little as $248, you just can't write off the older XM5s.

This Mashable Choice product received a 4.7 out of 5 stars in our original review, and even when we recently compared them head-to-head with their successors, they performed incredibly well.

We won't beat around the bush: There's no definitive "best" product here. Sure, elite audio brands put out high-quality products across the board, but even within each of those brands, you'll find different tiers of products. Some will deliver better value, and some will deliver better hardware and active noise cancellation.

In a recent development, all this to say, the best pair of earbuds or headphones largely comes down to personal preference and how you proposal to use them. Some listeners swear by over-ear headphones, while others prefer the minimalism of earbuds — one is not necessarily better than the other. Athletes who like to use headphones at the gym will appreciate waterproof materials and the best open earbuds, while frequent fliers will prefer devices with long battery life, comfort, and portability. Finally, music lovers and audiophiles will want to invest in premium features like a custom equalizer, spatial audio, or best-in-class active noise cancellation.

Industry observers note that to help you pick your pair, we tested all of the headphones in this guide (and a lot that didn't make the cut). Here, you'll find the top headphones of 2026 for noise cancellation, music, price, and wired connections.

Industry observers note that we focused primarily on the best wireless headphones for this guide. While wired headphones have their fans, wireless headphones are just more convenient for most of us, though some of us are also fans of Apple's EarPods. With the release of the new noise-cancelling wired earbuds from Bose, we will be keeping our testing pool open to more wired models and will enhancement this guide accordingly, should any earn a spot.

We tested the Marshall Monitor III and JBL Tour One M3 headphones, and though they had their merits, they fell short of winning the best of the best spot on this guide. We also tested the social media-famous Daisy One headphones, which have impeccable design, but fall flatter when it comes to sound and ANC quality.

We've also tested the Sonos Ace headphones and Dyson OnTrac headphones. And while we loved them both for sound quality and noise cancellation, they fare in the way of AirPods Max — left out of our recommendations for their high price points.

November 2026: We've replaced the Sony WH-CH720N with the newer WH-CH730N.

August 2026: Following the release of the second-generation Bose QuietComfort headphones, we've added them to our list as the best budget pick from Bose for headphones.

March 2025: We've designated the Bose QuietComfort Ultra 2 earbuds as the most comfortable ANC earbuds and crowned the Sony XM6 earbuds as the new best noise-cancelling earbuds.

December 2025: We replaced the Jabra Elite 8 Active Gen 2 earbuds, which are no longer available, with the Beats Powerbeats Pro 2 sports earbuds.

December 2025: We removed the Marshall Mode wired earbuds, as they're frequently out of stock.

December 2025: We added the Sony WH-CH720N Noise-Canceling Headphones as the best headphones under $100.

December 2025: We added the Sony XM5 headphones, originally released in 2022, as our latest honorable mention pick.

August 2026: We replaced the Sennheiser Momentum 4 with the Nothing Headphone (a) as our best battery life pick.

A few major headphone releases happened in September: Sony's mid-range WH-10000XM4C headphones, Sony's budget WH-CH730N headphones, and the Beats 360, the first pair of over-ear headphones from the brand in three years. Sony also released the original Walkman-inspired MDR-3R headphones in early November.

It has been revealed that no, we didn't forget to include the iconic Apple AirPods Max in our guide to the best headphones. It's not that we don't like them — in fact, we think they sound and look great (emphasis on look). However, after testing and re-testing them, we think they're just too expensive to justify a wholehearted recommendation. While we appreciate that they now (finally) come with lossless audio, they're still behind on features like battery life.

Industry observers note that while they're still a smart choice for style-conscious Apple fans, we can no longer include them among the elite. We thought they were way too expensive upon their initial release, and we only feel more firm in this position six years later.

While the long-anticipated AirPods Max 2 are finally out, our reviewer found the upgrades to be minimal. At the same $549 the original Maxes were released at, these headphones are just too expensive and underperforming for us to recommend them.

Sources indicate that like with most products, this comes down to personal preference, but there are a few brands known for making really solid headphones. For those who appreciate quality ANC above all else, Bose headphones will be the best brand. Enjoy a rich and balanced sound profile? You'll want to check out Sony. In the budget space, Anker Soundcore products have impressed us lately. Still, we recommend reading each of our above picks to see which speaks most to you.

In a recent development, if you're wondering what headphones you've been seeing all over your For You page, it's likely a pair of Sonys, either the older WH-1000XM5s or the brand newly introduced Sony WH-1000XM6s. The former two used to be our top picks, but the XM6s now take the crown. Beats headphones are also incredibly popular, especially as brands like Marshall and Jabra fall out of favor.

Other than those, the Bose QuietComfort line is a popular pick, especially for those who wear their headphones for long periods of time. And of course, Apple AirPods are a popular pick for iPhone users who prefer earbuds over headphones. We're not huge fans of the AirPods Max, though, as we think they're too overpriced for what they offer. However, with Apple's recent updates to the AirPods line, we know they are top of mind.

Every single pair of headphones we included in this guide was hands-on tested by a Mashable reporter, editor, or contributor. You can learn about our in-depth process by taking a look at the standardized testing guide we developed for this category.

Below, you'll find our condensed testing criteria for headphones:.

Sources indicate that we listened to a wide variety of genres of music, podcasts, and other forms of media. If a pair didn't at least sound solid across the board, they didn't make our list. In this category, we also considered the quality (and existence) of any equalizers.

We'll test ANC power around our homes as we work, with and without an audio assist, and outdoors. If headphones have customizable ANC levels, or automatic switching between noise-cancelling modes, we make sure that they actually provide noticeable differences in performance.

According to recent reports, everything from comfort to touch controls fall under this category. We look at what headphones offer to provide the best wear for the greatest amount of people, whether that be a strong selection of earbud tip sizes or particularly soft padding. Whenever possible, we test and re-test headphones over longer periods of time to see how they hold up.

We evaluate how headphones perform in all of the above categories, and if that performance matches their price point.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dax Shepard is getting candid about his mental health amid controversy.

The Armchair Expert host shared he's experiencing depression over allegations that he's an "abusive husband" to his wife of 13 years Kristen Bell.

Industry observers note that "I generally don't have depression, but I've had it," Shepard shared on the Nov. 23 episode of his podcast. "I'm so tired and I've been taking so many naps, and I got to say there that is a silver lining.".

The 51-year-old went on to describe the "continuing narrative" that he allegedly mistreats his wife as "very offensive," noting how the accusations first started last year when some social media consumers misconstrued an inside joke the Frozen star had made in an Instagram post celebrating their wedding anniversary.

"We were watching Dateline one time, and everyone kills their rich spouse," Shepard recounted to guest Zosia Mamet, explaining how he was "complimenting Kristen" by telling her at the time, "'You know, I’m heavily incentivized to kill you, but I’m not going to.’".

Though Bell had told him that the quip was "one of the most romantic things anyone remarked to her," Shepard said a "cottage industry of women" online didn't think so and accused him of being a "dangerous man.".

And when Bell recently revealed that her husband unconventionally flirts with her by complimenting other people while in her presence, Shepard mentioned the allegations that he's a "controlling" spouse only snowballed.

"Of course, the controlling husband would try to control the narrative," Shepard sarcastically remarked, before agreeing to Mamet's assessment that he's "f--ked.".

In fact, Shepard has emphatically denied claims that he mistreats Bell, with whom he shares two daughters.

Industry observers note that "I don't ever yell at my children. I don't swear at them. I don't yell at my wife," he mentioned on Armchair Expert's Nov. 9 episode. "To have given it my all to be the opposite of what, now, some group of people is saying I am is hard.".

"I find it deeply insulting to my wife, additionally," Shepard added. "She's sitting in a house with her two daughters and modeling some abusive relationship? It's very offensive to her.".

For a real look at Shepard and Bell's home life with their kids, read on.

'Star Trek: First Contact' at 30: Resistance is futile when it comes to the 'Next Generation' crew's greatest significant-screen adventure

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1882 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard.
  • Recent findings suggest that with the Borg overrunning the newly rolled out USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat.
  • But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following the sad news of Sir Patrick Stewart's passing, there's been no shortage of discussion about his best moments as Captain Jean-Luc Picard. "The Inner Light"'s life in 25 minutes is a strong contender, as are the courtroom grandstanding in "The Measure of a Man" and his insistence (under extreme torture) that "there are four lights!" in "Chain of Command". But for this writer's money, it's hard to look past a nine-minute sequence in "Star Trek: First Contact", which turns 30 this weekend.

Recent findings suggest that with the Borg overrunning the newly rolled out USS Enterprise-E, Picard — who has long-standing beef with the Collective, following his assimilation in classic "The Next Generation" story "The Best of Both Worlds" — orders his crew to fight the cybernetic nasties hand-to-hand if required, defying their pleas to activate the ship's self-destruct system and retreat. He even calls Worf — not a man renowned for dodging a fight — a coward, prompting the Klingon to respond that, "If you were any other man, I would kill you where you stand." Ouch.

But following some impassioned talk about making the Borg "pay for what they've done", he's finally talked down from his rage by 21st-century stowaway Lily Sloane (Alfre Woodard). She points out that his Moby-Dick-esque obsession is on the verge of going full Ahab, and he eventually sees sense, issuing the order to abandon the Enterprise and destroy the hive.

It's a masterclass showcasing the ever-brilliant Stewart's impressive range, as the out-of-control captain's rarely seen temper reaches fever pitch, before normal service is resumed. His subsequent apology to Worf — "As a matter of fact, I think you're the bravest man I've ever known" — is simply perfect.

And just as the franchise's zenith, "The Wrath of Khan", is built around Kirk and Khan's decades-old feud, "First Contact" is precision engineered to get the most out of Jean-Luc. This was the right "Star Trek" at the right time, a film that put "TNG"'s greatest villains on a collision course with the origins of Starfleet. It's not quite "Khan", of course — what is? — but it deserves to be mentioned in the same breath.

In 1996, the "odd numbers bad, even numbers good" rule of "Trek" films still, more or less, rang true. 1994's "Generations", rushed out a few months after "The Next Generation" ended its seven-year run on TV, had done decent business, but the seventh movie's convoluted "passing the baton" storyline had left many fans cold. Now, however, with Kirk killed off, it was time for Picard and his crew to explore the big-screen frontier alone.

It has been revealed that william Shatner actually pitched a resurrection storyline for Kirk, but "Trek" executive producer/overlord Rick Berman ruled that it was a little too soon to bring the good captain back. Instead, he hired "Generations" scripters and "TNG"/"Deep Space Nine" writers' room regulars Brannon Braga and Ronald D. Moore to craft an eighth movie capable of living up to its even-numbered predecessors.

Recent findings suggest that while "Generations" had been written to an extremely restrictive brief, Braga and Moore were given much more freedom the second time out. Berman was keen on a time-travel storyline while Braga lobbied for the fan-favorite Borg, and early on they explored the idea of taking the Collective back to Renaissance Italy. These aims were abandoned when Stewart vetoed the idea of wearing tights.

They eventually zeroed in on April 5, 2063, the date Zefram Cochrane (a character who'd previously appeared in Original Series episode "Metamorphosis") made humanity's first warp flight and put Earth on the radar of a passing Vulcan ship.

"We landed on the idea of what I called the 'Star Trek' nativity scene — the birth of 'Star Trek'," Braga said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Mark A Altman and Edward Gross.

Sources indicate that "The three wise Vulcans who arrive on Earth and step out of their ship for our first contact with an extraterrestrial species. And the Borg were going to prevent that from happening, which really struck a bullseye for me, because it would allow non-'Star Trek' people to understand why 'Star Trek' matters by putting the crew and the Borg back in that time frame. I thought it would appeal to a larger audience. 'Star Trek' itself was at stake, and that was super cool to me.".

Paramount reportedly flirted with significant-name directors like Ridley Scott ("Alien", "Blade Runner") and John McTiernan ("Predator", "Die Hard"), before settling on Jonathan Frakes. Although this would be Frakes' first movie, the man best known for playing Commander Riker had directed numerous "Trek" episodes. Berman believed that an understanding of the franchise's DNA was more notable than big-screen experience.

The film wastes little time on exposition for "Trek" newbies, with just a short dream sequence to explain away Picard's history with the Borg. With a single Borg Cube on course for Earth, the Federation fleet mobilizes to fight them off. They're getting their asses well and truly kicked, too, until the Enterprise warps into the battle.

The Cube is ultimately destroyed but still manages to dispatch a Sphere, which uses chronometric particles to travel back to 2063 in order to assimilate Earth in the past. Picard has no choice but to follow them back to "repair whatever damage they've done".

In a recent development, they arrive in a post-World War III Montana, where Cochrane has constructed his prototype faster-than-light vessel, the Phoenix. Played by "Babe" star James Cromwell (who'd already guest-starred in a trio of "TNG" episodes), Cochrane is some way from the man future history has remembered: a hard-drinking womanizer more motivated by potential riches than the betterment of mankind. A man uncomfortable with the idea that a high school will one day bear his name.

But as some of the crew work to repair the damage caused by the Sphere's bombing raid, there are bigger problems in orbit. Borg survivors have beamed on board the Enterprise and started assimilating the vessel and its crew.

Initial drafts of the script saw Riker leading the ship-based resistance while Picard remained on Earth, but — at Stewart's request — Braga and Moore flipped things round to bring the captain face-to-face with his nemesis. It proved to be a really smart move, as Stewart got to ditch his latest-look Starfleet uniform and run around the Enterprise as a full-on action hero in a John McClane-style vest.

It has been revealed that these Borg had been given a multiplex upgrade, with massively improved prosthetics and newly introduced extendable tendrils that injected nanoprobes to assimilate a victim from within. Frakes played up the horror aspects of the Collective, portraying them as a horde of mindless cybernetic zombies, while using "Alien" and "Aliens" as inspiration.

"[Ridley Scott and James Cameron] made it clear that when it comes to villains, the more that's suggested, the scarier they are," Frakes explained. "I tried to get that with the Borg.".

The biggest change came at the head of the organization, where — at the suggestion of Paramount executive Jonathan Dolgen — "First Contact" introduced a previously unseen Borg Queen (brilliantly played by Alice Krige) to act as spokesperson for the Collective.

Recent findings suggest that bringing a singular entity to a civilisation built on the notion that there's no "I" in "team" was a controversial move, but it made perfect dramatic sense. Indeed, a legion of drones would have little chance of seducing Data, even if it was just for 0.68 seconds.

In a recent development, "We wrestled with it quite a bit before we committed to [the Borg Queen's] character," Moore told Syfy Wire, "because it was a choice that was also antithetical to the idea of the Borg. The whole concept of these villains was that they were a collection, and that there were no individuals. And that's what made them the faceless, implacable 'resistance is futile' enemy. But it also limited how to deal with them dramatically because it meant that any scenes you always had to deal with this sort of collective voice. We decided that the story would be better if we had some individual to deal with.".

The Queen was also granted one of the greatest entrances in sci-fi history, as her head and torso were lowered into a robot body with a bit of help from Industrial Light & Magic.

It has been revealed that the Starfleet armada's assault on the Borg was similarly impressive and effectively a test run for "The Phantom Menace", as ILM's visual effects supervisor John Knoll pioneered the CG effects pipeline that would later become pivotal to the "Star Wars" prequels. It was also a brilliant excuse to introduce several newly introduced starship designs to the "Trek" canon.

They're standout moments in a film that made the most of its comparatively puny budget of $45 million (reported). (For comparison, "Independence Day", which was released the same year — and also featured Brent Spiner — cost closer to $75 million.).

Sources indicate that as Moore later recalled in an interview with the Hollywood Reporter, "Paramount had their formula. They said that 'Star Trek' movies only make this amount of money. So, therefore, you can only have this amount of budget to make it. And, at that point, we were still — just like on the TV show — counting phaser beam effects shots [to keep the price down].".

The studio needn't have worried. "First Contact" was a huge hit with fans and became one of the franchise's highest-grossing films at the box office. Borg mythology introduced here (including the Queen) would become a mainstay on "Star Trek: Voyager", while Jean-Luc would get to face his cybernetic white whale again in "Picard" — though the incomparable Stewart arguably never again had another "Trek" scene to rival the ones he had here.

Industry observers note that "Fortunately it happened to be a wonderful script, and my job was not to screw it up," said Frakes. "It also holds up as a movie that just happens to be a 'Star Trek' movie, which we were all hoping would be the case.".

'Star Trek: First Contact' is available to stream on Paramount+ in the US and the UK.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup.
  • Two of the upcoming studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal vital differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Recent findings suggest that researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease.

Two of the upcoming studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto).

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an crucial period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio).

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation.

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

It has been revealed that in a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati).

Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota).

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders.

Recent findings suggest that together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

Recent findings suggest that "These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," stated Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders.".

Musk's Twitter promised a purge of blue check marks. Instead he singled out the New York Times
